questions.q: Why does reading the 5,000th item of a linked list cost O(n), when it is O(1) in an array?
questions.explain: An array computes the slot's address from the index. A list only knows its head, so reaching item i takes i steps.
options: Linked lists store items as strings
Nodes are not side by side in memory, so there is no address formula; you must follow 4,999 next pointers from the head
JavaScript copies the list on every read

questions.q: You hold a reference to a node in the middle of a 100,000-node singly linked list. What does inserting a new node right after it cost?
questions.explain: Nothing shifts in a linked list. That is its main advantage over an array, where inserting in the middle moves every later item.
options: O(1): create the node and rewire two next pointers
O(n): the list must be copied

questions.q: A singly linked list keeps both head and tail. Why is removing the last node still O(n)?
questions.explain: A prev pointer (a doubly linked list) makes this O(1). Adding at the back and removing at the front are O(1) either way.
options: The new tail must be the node before the old tail, and a singly linked node does not know its predecessor, so you walk from the head to find it
Because the garbage collector must visit every node
It is O(1) with a tail pointer

questions.q: Which pair of operations turns a singly linked list with a tail into an O(1) queue?
questions.explain: Adding at the tail and removing at the head are both O(1). The last option is a stack (LIFO), and the first two need the O(n) remove-last.
options: pushFront to enqueue and remove-last to dequeue
pushBack to enqueue and remove-last to dequeue

questions.q: A popFront sets this.head = node.next but never touches this.tail. What goes wrong after popping the only node?
questions.explain: When the list becomes empty, both head and tail must become null. One-node and empty lists are where most linked list bugs hide.
options: head is null but tail still points at the removed node, so the next pushBack links the new node onto a node that is no longer in the list, and the list looks empty

questions.q: In the in-place reversal, why must const next = current.next run before current.next = previous?
questions.explain: Turning the arrow around destroys the only link forward. Save it first, then rewire, then advance.
options: Once current.next is overwritten, nothing points to the rest of the list any more; without the saved reference the loop cannot continue and the remaining nodes are lost
It can run in either order

questions.q: A recursive reversal is only a few lines long. What does it cost compared with the loop?
questions.explain: Each recursive call waits for the next one, so all n frames exist at once. The three-pointer loop uses O(1) extra space.
options: The same: O(n) time, O(1) space
O(n) time but O(n) space: one call stack frame per node, which overflows on very long lists

questions.q: The Set-based cycle detector stores node objects, not approver names. Why?
questions.explain: Sets compare objects by identity, which is exactly "have I been at this node before?". Names would report false cycles.
options: Two different approvers can share a name; only revisiting the same node means the chain loops
Objects are faster to hash than strings

questions.q: In Floyd's cycle detection, why must the fast pointer eventually land on the slow one when there is a cycle?
questions.explain: A gap that shrinks by one per step cannot jump over zero. Without a cycle, the fast pointer simply reaches null.
options: Because the fast pointer slows down inside the cycle
Once both are in the cycle, each step the fast pointer gains exactly one node on the slow one, so the gap shrinks by one each step until it is zero
It does not always; it only usually meets

questions.q: What is the main advantage of Floyd's algorithm over the Set version?
questions.explain: Both are O(n) time and both are correct. Floyd's needs only two pointers, which matters for huge lists or many checks.
options: It finds cycles the Set version misses
O(1) extra space instead of O(n)

questions.q: An admin can set any approver's "next approver". What is the best way to handle cycles in the approval chain?
questions.explain: Validating at write time stops bad data entering the system. Defensive reads protect against data that got in anyway.
options: Walk the chain with a for loop and hope
Check for a cycle before saving the change and reject it, and keep walkers defensive so they stop with an error instead of looping
Limit the chain to two approvers
Restart the server when it hangs

questions.q: What does the extra prev pointer in a doubly linked list buy you?
questions.explain: It costs one more pointer per node. In return, removing a node never needs a search for its predecessor, which is what an LRU cache relies on.
options: O(1) removal of any node you hold, because both neighbours are reachable from it

questions.q: Why does the doubly linked list use two permanent dummy (sentinel) nodes?
questions.explain: With sentinels, remove is always the same two pointer updates. Without them, removing the first or last node needs extra branches, a common source of bugs.
options: Every real node always has a real prev and next, so insert and remove never need special cases for an empty list, the head or the tail
To speed up the garbage collector

questions.q: remove(node) sets node.prev = node.next = null after unlinking it. What does that protect against?
questions.explain: A second remove on a detached node now throws a TypeError (reading next of null) instead of silently breaking other nodes.
options: A caller that keeps a stale reference and calls remove on it again would otherwise rewire live neighbours and corrupt the list; with nulls it fails loudly instead
It is required for the size to be correct

questions.q: In the LRU cache, what is the Map for, and what is the doubly linked list for?
questions.explain: Neither is enough alone: a list cannot find a key without scanning, and (conceptually) a plain hash map has no order. Together every operation is O(1).
options: The map keeps the order; the list finds keys
The map finds a key's node in O(1); the list keeps nodes in recency order so moving and evicting are O(1)
Both store the same thing for safety

questions.q: Why does each list node in the LRU store its key, not only its value?
questions.explain: Eviction starts from the list (the least recently used node) and must clean up the map too. Without the key in the node, you would need an O(n) search of the map.
options: When the last node is evicted, the cache must also delete that key from the map, and the node is the only place to read it from

questions.q: In an LRU cache, why must get move the entry to the front?
questions.explain: "Least recently used" means reads count. The trace in the lesson shows RICE surviving an eviction only because it was read again.
options: Reading a product is a "use"; if get did not update the order, a product read constantly would still be evicted as if it were unused

questions.q: A price changes in the pricing service but the LRU cache keeps serving the old one for hours, because the product is popular. What is missing?
questions.explain: Eviction and freshness are separate policies. Popular entries never get evicted, so they need a time limit or an explicit delete when the source changes.
options: Expiry (a TTL) or invalidation on change; LRU only decides what to evict when the cache is full
Nothing; that is correct LRU behaviour and cannot be changed

questions.q: A popular product's cache entry expires, and 500 requests for it arrive in the next 100 ms. With a simple cache, each misses and calls the pricing service. What is the usual fix?
questions.explain: This is a cache stampede. Sharing one in-flight request per key turns 500 service calls into 1.
options: Cache the pending promise of the first call, so the other requests wait for it instead of starting their own

questions.q: Summing a million numbers takes O(n) in both an array and a linked list, yet the array is many times faster. Why?
questions.explain: Big O ignores memory layout. In practice, cache locality often decides, which is why arrays are the default and linked lists are used for their O(1) moves.
options: Array items are contiguous, so the CPU cache loads many at once; list nodes can be scattered, so each step may wait for main memory, and every node also carries extra memory overhead
Linked lists are O(n²) to traverse

questions.q: How can you build an LRU cache in JavaScript with only a Map?
questions.explain: Maps iterate in insertion order, and re-inserting moves a key to the end. Both steps are O(1), so this is a real, short LRU in JavaScript.
options: It is impossible without a linked list
On every use, delete the key and set it again so it moves to the end of the insertion order; evict map.keys().next().value, the oldest key
Sort the map's keys on every access

questions.q: A product cache has 2,000 hits and 8,000 misses per hour. What does this suggest?
questions.explain: Hit rate = hits / (hits + misses). Measure it before and after changing capacity or key design; a cache that rarely hits is mostly overhead.
options: A 20% hit rate: the cache is too small for the working set, or its keys are too specific, so it costs memory while saving little

questions.explain: Each new node becomes the head and points at the previous head, so this builds the list by pushing at the front: the last one added comes first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every arrow is turned around. When current becomes null, previous is the old last node, which is the new head.

questions.q: This reversal forgets to save next. What does it print?
questions.explain: After current.next = previous, reading current.next gives previous (null on the first step), so the loop stops after one node, and B and C are lost.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Ada → Bola → null has no cycle. Pointing Bola back at Ada creates one, and the pointers meet. An empty chain has no cycle.

questions.q: An LRU cache with capacity 2 (the least recently used key is evicted when a third arrives). What does this print?
questions.explain: Using RICE again moves it to the end, so OIL becomes the oldest and is evicted when SALT arrives. The Map's order is oldest first.

questions.q: Same cache, capacity 2. Which key is evicted and what remains?
questions.explain: C evicts A; then A evicts B; then B evicts C. With a capacity smaller than the set of keys used in a cycle, LRU evicts every key just before it is needed again: the worst case for LRU.

questions.q: This removal loop advances previous even after unlinking. What does it print?
questions.explain: After unlinking the first cancelled node, the loop moves on to the second cancelled node without checking it: the same skipped-item bug as splice in a forward array loop. Only advance when you did not unlink.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For six nodes, the fast pointer stops at null after three steps, leaving the slow pointer on the fourth node (the second of the two middles). For three nodes it stops on the second.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Removing A only rewires the head sentinel and B. Walking backwards from the tail sentinel gives C, B, and the first real node is now B.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When one list runs out, the rest of the other is already sorted and is attached in one step. O(n + m) time and no new nodes.

questions.q: Write toArray(head) that walks a singly linked list and returns its values in order.
questions.explain: Start at the head and follow next until null. The empty list is just null, so the loop never runs.

questions.q: Finish pushBack and popFront for a list with head, tail and size. Both must be O(1) and keep head and tail correct when the list becomes empty or has one node.
questions.explain: An empty list needs head set on the first push, and popping the last node must clear tail. A complete version would also throw when popping an empty list.
questions.expected:
J-1 J-2 0 null null
J-3 J-3 1

questions.q: Write reverse(head) in place with O(1) extra space and return the new head.
questions.explain: Save next, turn the arrow, advance both pointers. The loop handles the empty list by never running and returning null.

questions.q: Write hasCycle(head) with Floyd's slow and fast pointers, using O(1) extra space.
questions.explain: Check fast and fast.next before moving two steps, or a list of even length throws on null.next. Compare nodes with ===, not their values.

questions.q: Write remove(node) for a doubly linked list with sentinels: unlink the node in O(1) and clear its own prev and next.
questions.explain: The neighbours skip over the node in both directions. Thanks to the sentinels, the same two lines work for the first, last and only node.

questions.q: Build an LRU cache with only a Map: get must mark the key as recently used, and set must evict the least recently used key when the size goes over capacity.
questions.explain: Delete and re-set moves a key to the end of the Map's insertion order; the first key is the least recently used. Reading RICE saved it, so OIL was evicted.

questions.q: Find the k-th transaction from the end of a singly linked list in one pass (k = 1 is the last), using two pointers k nodes apart. Return null if the list is shorter than k.
questions.explain: Move the lead pointer k nodes ahead, then move both until the lead falls off the end: the trail is k from the end. One pass, O(1) space.

questions.q: Write totalPaid(head) that walks a list of orders and returns the total kobo of the orders whose status is "paid".
questions.explain: A linked list is traversed just like an array with a loop, following next instead of increasing an index. O(n) time, O(1) space.
